title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Athens and a wood outside it, over four days and one very long night
lengthNote: Around 2,100 lines, with four separate companies of characters to keep in the air
openingLine: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour Draws on apace
summary: A father asks the Duke of Athens to have his daughter killed if she will not marry the man he has chosen, and the comedy proceeds from there. Four young people run into a wood where a quarrelling fairy king and queen are already using a drug that makes the sleeper love whatever they see first, and a company of Athenian tradesmen are rehearsing a tragedy they cannot act. The play's interest is that magic does not invent the lovers' cruelty to one another; it only speeds it up.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of A Midsummer Night's Dream
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Modern editions based on the 1600 quarto may differ by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Usually placed close to Romeo and Juliet, whose plot the mechanicals accidentally perform as farce.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed for Thomas Fisher, whose title page says the play had been publicly acted by the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Ovid, Chaucer, English fairy lore and Shakespeare's own theatre, combined rather than adapted.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Court, lovers, fairies and players, each with a different kind of verse.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A law, a deadline and a cast list
structure.summary: Theseus is four days from marrying a woman he defeated in battle when Egeus arrives demanding the Athenian law that lets a father dispose of a daughter. Hermia is given a month to obey, die or enter a convent; she and Lysander agree to run, tell Helena, and Helena tells Demetrius. In a separate room six tradesmen are allocating parts in a play about a double suicide.

scenes.title: The law
scenes.summary: Egeus demands his right; Theseus upholds it; the lovers plan to escape and Helena betrays the plan.

scenes.title: The casting
scenes.summary: Quince hands out parts and Bottom offers to play all of them.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A quarrel that has spoiled the weather
structure.summary: Oberon and Titania have fallen out over a stolen Indian boy, and the dispute has stopped the seasons behaving. Oberon sends for a flower whose juice makes the sleeper dote on whatever they first see, intending it for his wife, and adds an instruction about the Athenian youth he has just watched treat a woman badly. Puck anoints the wrong Athenian.

scenes.title: The flower
scenes.summary: Oberon and Titania quarrel; Helena pursues Demetrius through the wood; Puck is sent for love-in-idleness.

scenes.title: The mistake
scenes.summary: Titania is drugged asleep; Puck finds Lysander and Hermia lying apart and anoints the wrong man.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Everything wrong at once
structure.summary: Bottom acquires an ass's head, his friends run, and the fairy queen wakes and falls in love with him. In the other half of the wood both men now love Helena, who is certain she is being mocked, and the two women who grew up together insult each other's height until the men go off to fight. Oberon has Puck fog the wood and put them all to sleep.

scenes.title: The ass's head
scenes.summary: The rehearsal is interrupted; Bottom is transformed and Titania wakes to adore him.

scenes.title: The quarrel
scenes.summary: Both men court Helena, the two women fall out, and Puck leads the rivals astray in the dark.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Waking up, and not asking questions
structure.summary: Oberon has what he wanted, releases Titania and says nothing about how he got it. Theseus finds the four lovers asleep in the wood, overrules Egeus and adds them to his own wedding — while Demetrius, alone of the four, is still under the drug. Bottom wakes last, in the middle of the stage, trying to describe something he has no words for.

scenes.title: The waking
scenes.summary: Titania is released; the hunt finds the lovers; Theseus overrules the law; Bottom wakes and gropes for his dream.

scenes.title: Back in Athens
scenes.summary: The players mourn their lost leading man until he walks in with news of a wedding.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The worst play ever performed, and a blessing
structure.summary: Three couples watch Pyramus and Thisbe, a tragedy of forbidden love and mistaken death performed by men who explain the wall and apologise for the lion. The court heckles it; the play they are mocking is the story they have just escaped. The fairies then come indoors to bless the marriages, and Puck asks the audience to call the whole thing a dream.

scenes.title: Pyramus and Thisbe, and the epilogue
scenes.summary: The mechanicals perform; the court comments; Oberon and Titania bless the house; Puck asks for pardon.

characters.name: Theseus
characters.summary: He begins by upholding a law that would kill a girl for choosing the wrong husband and ends by overruling it without explanation, having changed nothing about his beliefs in between. His great speech dismisses lovers, lunatics and poets as the same kind of unreliable witness, which is spoken in a play that has just shown the audience fairies.
characters.clue: He won his bride in battle, tells a girl her father made her as a seal makes an impression in wax, and does not believe a word of what the lovers report.

characters.name: Hippolyta
characters.role: Queen of the Amazons, betrothed to Theseus
characters.summary: She says very little and almost all of it disagrees with her future husband. When he explains away the lovers' night as imagination, she points out that four people telling the same story is evidence of something, which is the only argument in the play for believing the audience's own eyes.

characters.name: Egeus
characters.summary: He appears twice, asks for his daughter's death both times, and is then simply overruled and forgotten. Shakespeare gives the comedy's opening crisis to a man with no interior life at all, so that the law he invokes looks like a piece of machinery rather than a feeling.

characters.name: Hermia
characters.role: Egeus's daughter, in love with Lysander
characters.summary: Threatened with death in the first scene, she argues back in front of a duke and then leaves the city. In the wood she loses her certainty piece by piece — first her lover, then her oldest friend — and the play's harshest comedy is about her height, which is the one thing she cannot answer.
characters.clue: Ordered to marry a man she does not want or die, she runs; by dawn she is being called a bead, an acorn and a painted maypole by her closest friend.

characters.name: Lysander
characters.role: An Athenian in love with Hermia
characters.summary: He is Demetrius's equal in everything except the father's approval, which is the whole plot. Drugged, he turns on Hermia with a viciousness the spell does not really account for, and the play never gives him a line acknowledging what he said.

characters.name: Helena
characters.role: In love with Demetrius, who has abandoned her
characters.summary: She betrays her friend's escape plan in order to be thanked by a man who despises her, and knows exactly how little that is worth while she does it. Her offer to be treated like a dog is the most uncomfortable speech in the comedy, and when both men suddenly want her she assumes it is a joke at her expense.
characters.clue: She hands over her best friend's secret to a man who has just told her he is sick when he looks at her, and asks only to be beaten and followed like a spaniel.

characters.name: Demetrius
characters.summary: He courted Helena, dropped her, and threatens her with violence in the wood when she will not stop following him. He is the only one of the four never released from the drug: the comedy's final pairing rests on an enchantment nobody on stage mentions again.

relationships.label: abandoned, then restored to by magic

characters.name: Oberon
characters.summary: He wants a boy his wife is raising and drugs her into humiliation until she gives him up. The same night he also takes pity on a woman he has never met and tries to fix her love life, and the play makes no attempt to reconcile the two impulses in one character.
characters.clue: He watches everything from the edge of the stage, corrects one couple out of pity and destroys his wife's dignity to win an argument about a child.

characters.name: Titania
characters.summary: Her account of the ruined seasons makes the fairy quarrel a matter of flooded fields and human disease, which is a larger claim than any other character makes for themselves. She keeps the changeling boy out of loyalty to his dead mother, and loses him while drugged into loving a weaver with an ass's head.
characters.clue: She keeps a dead friend's child, blames the rotted corn and the drowned fields on her marriage, and wakes to find herself feeding apricots to a man with an ass's head.

characters.name: Puck
characters.summary: He belongs to English village folklore rather than to Athens, and he is brought into the play as both an employee and a hazard: he does what he is told and enjoys what goes wrong with it. He is given the last word, and uses it to offer the audience a way out of everything they have seen.
characters.clue: He frightens village girls, curdles the milk, mistakes one Athenian for another, and finally asks the audience to pretend they were asleep.

characters.name: Nick Bottom
characters.summary: He wants to play every part in the play and is the only mortal who meets the fairies awake and is not frightened of them. He is also the only one who tries to describe the night afterwards, and the speech in which he fails — senses swapped over, words giving out — is the play's most serious statement about what has happened to everyone.
characters.clue: A weaver who offers to play the lion, the lady and the tyrant, is given an ass's head, and wakes up trying to say what his eye has heard.

themes.name: Love without reason
themes.summary: The play's working definition of love is that it cannot be argued with and cannot be trusted: Helena says it looks with the mind rather than the eyes, Bottom observes that reason and love keep little company, and a flower produces the same effect as a lifetime's devotion. What the drug does is not unnatural; it is only quicker.
themes.development: Stated as theory in 1.1, demonstrated on the lovers in Acts II and III, and left standing at the end with Demetrius still under the influence.

themes.name: Law, fathers and consent
themes.summary: Athens opens with a father asking a duke to enforce his right to kill his daughter, and the duke agreeing that this is the law. Nothing in the last act repeals it — Theseus simply stops applying it, which leaves the comedy's happy ending resting on a ruler's mood.
themes.development: Egeus makes his demand in 1.1 and repeats it in 4.1; Theseus overrules him without argument, and Egeus is given nothing further to say.

themes.name: Transformation
themes.summary: Everyone in the wood is altered and almost nobody notices at the time. The one visible change, Bottom's head, is the least distressing of them: it is the invisible changes — a man waking to loathe the woman he loved — that the play treats as frightening.
themes.development: Titania is drugged in 2.2, Lysander in the same scene, Bottom transformed in 3.1; three of the four are undone by 4.1 and the fourth is not.

themes.name: Night, sleep and the morning story
themes.summary: The play's settlement depends on everybody agreeing to call the night a dream. Theseus produces the sceptical account, Hippolyta doubts it, Bottom cannot fit his experience into words, and Puck finally offers the whole audience the same bargain.
themes.development: The lovers wake half-remembering in 4.1; Theseus explains it away in 5.1; the epilogue makes the explanation the audience's responsibility.

themes.name: Theatre about theatre
themes.summary: The mechanicals worry about the things real companies worry about — casting, props, whether the audience will be frightened, whether a boy can play a woman — and solve them by explaining everything aloud. Their failure demonstrates the conventions the surrounding play is relying on at that exact moment.
themes.development: Rehearsal in 1.2 and 3.1, performance in 5.1, and an epilogue that asks the same indulgence the mechanicals begged for in their prologue.

themes.name: Who is allowed to decide
themes.summary: Fathers, dukes and fairy kings all get what they want, and each of them frames it as correction rather than force. The play lets that pattern show by repeating it at three social levels within an hour of stage time.
themes.development: Egeus invokes the law, Theseus invokes his sword and his wedding, Oberon invokes a flower; the changeling boy changes hands offstage and is never mentioned again.

techniques.name: Verse registers
techniques.definition: Giving different groups of characters distinct metres and forms.
techniques.inThisBook: The court speaks blank verse, the lovers slide into rhymed couplets as they become more ridiculous, the fairies use a short trochaic line, and the mechanicals speak prose except when performing, where they are given deliberately terrible verse.

techniques.name: Play within a play
techniques.definition: A staged performance watched by characters who are themselves being watched.
techniques.inThisBook: Pyramus and Thisbe is a tragedy of parental prohibition and mistaken death, performed for four people who have just escaped one. The court's mockery is aimed at conventions the audience has been accepting all evening.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: One actor taking two parts, so that the audience sees a resemblance the text does not state.
techniques.inThisBook: Theseus and Oberon, Hippolyta and Titania, and Philostrate and Puck have often been doubled since Peter Brook's 1970 production, which turns the fairy quarrel into the same marriage seen at night.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A sudden drop from the elevated to the ridiculous.
techniques.inThisBook: It is the engine of the whole last act — 'the wall is down that parted their fathers' — and also of the wood, where a fairy queen's love speech is answered by a weaver talking about the difficulty of getting out of a wood.

techniques.name: The catalogue
techniques.definition: A list used to build a world faster than description can.
techniques.inThisBook: Oberon's bank of wild thyme, oxlips, violets, woodbine, musk-roses and eglantine gives the wood a physical existence on a bare stage in six lines, and Titania's list of rotted corn and drowned fields does the same for the damage.

techniques.name: Epilogue
techniques.definition: A direct address to the audience after the story has closed.
techniques.inThisBook: Puck offers the audience the same excuse the characters have used on themselves — that they were asleep and this was a dream — which makes accepting the comedy an act the spectators have to perform.

quotations.text: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour Draws on apace; four happy days bring in Another moon: but, O, methinks, how slow This old moon wanes!
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The opening lines, four days before the wedding.
quotations.analysis: The play starts a clock and immediately complains about it, which is how the whole comedy will run: everything is dated to the moon. The image Theseus reaches for — an old woman withering away a young man's inheritance — puts impatience and money in the first speech of a play about who may marry whom.

quotations.text: Hippolyta, I woo'd thee with my sword, And won thy love, doing thee injuries; But I will wed thee in another key,
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: To his bride, in the same opening speech.
quotations.analysis: He describes a conquest as a courtship without appearing to notice the difference, and 'doing thee injuries' is left in the sentence as a plain fact. 'In another key' is a musical term, so the change he promises is one of tone rather than of relation — which is precisely the question Oberon and Titania will act out in the wood.

quotations.text: I beg the ancient privilege of Athens, As she is mine, I may dispose of her: Which shall be either to this gentleman Or to her death, according to our law
quotations.speaker: Egeus
quotations.context: Asking the duke to enforce his right over his daughter.
quotations.analysis: 'Dispose of' is a term for property, and the alternatives offered are a husband or an execution, in that order and in the same sentence. Egeus is not presented as a monster: he is invoking something he calls ancient and the duke agrees it exists, which is what makes the first scene of a comedy cold.

quotations.text: To you your father should be as a god; One that composed your beauties, yea, and one To whom you are but as a form in wax By him imprinted and within his power To leave the figure or disfigure it.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Advising Hermia to obey, before setting out her choices.
quotations.analysis: The image makes a daughter a seal impression rather than a person, and the pun on figure and disfigure lets destruction sound like a matter of craft. It is offered as kindly counsel, which is the point: the play's cruelty is spoken in the register of good sense.

quotations.text: The course of true love never did run smooth;
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: Comforting Hermia after the duke's judgement.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted line in the play is a young man consoling his girlfriend by telling her that their situation is an old story, and he is about to list the ways love goes wrong as if reciting from a book. What follows is not comfort but a catalogue of obstacles, ending in the image of darkness swallowing light.

quotations.text: And ere a man hath power to say 'Behold!' The jaws of darkness do devour it up: So quick bright things come to confusion.
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: The end of his list of the ways love is thwarted.
quotations.analysis: Three heavy monosyllables — jaws, darkness, devour — arrive in a comedy fifteen minutes old. 'Quick' means living as well as fast, so the line describes both a flash of lightning and a short life, and it is the closest this play comes to the tragedy the mechanicals will perform badly in the last act.

quotations.text: Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind:
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Alone, deciding to betray Hermia's escape plan to Demetrius.
quotations.analysis: She works out the play's theory of love before any magic has appeared, and then acts on it in the worst available way. The rhymed couplets she has slipped into mark the moment a character stops talking to other people and starts constructing an argument for herself.

quotations.text: Let me play the lion too: I will roar, that I will do any man's heart good to hear me;
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: At the casting, having already asked to play Pyramus and Thisbe.
quotations.analysis: 'Too' is the joke: he has accepted the lead and wants the other parts as well, including the one with no words. Quince talks him out of it by explaining that a convincing lion would get the company hanged, which is the first of the play's several reminders that theatre in 1595 was a licensed activity.

quotations.text: Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: The first meeting of the fairy king and queen in the play.
quotations.analysis: Six words establish that this marriage is in the middle of a long argument, and the greeting inverts a courtesy — well met — into its opposite. Everything the fairies do for the rest of the night is a move in a quarrel that began before the audience arrived.

quotations.text: And thorough this distemperature we see The seasons alter: hoary-headed frosts Far in the fresh lap of the crimson rose,
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: In the middle of her account of the damage the quarrel has done.
quotations.analysis: The speech puts flooded fields, rotted corn and human disease on the domestic argument's account, which is a far larger claim than any mortal in the play makes. It also dates the comedy for the first audience: the mid-1590s were years of ruined harvests and abnormal weather, and this is the play noticing.

quotations.text: Set your heart at rest: The fairy land buys not the child of me. His mother was a votaress of my order:
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Refusing to hand over the changeling boy.
quotations.analysis: Her reason for keeping the child is not possessiveness but a promise to a dead friend, and the speech that follows is the warmest thing in the play — two women laughing on a beach at the shape of the sails. The boy himself never appears, and after Act IV nobody mentions him again.

quotations.text: It fell upon a little western flower, Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound, And maidens call it love-in-idleness.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: Describing how Cupid's arrow missed an imperial votaress and struck a flower.
quotations.analysis: The drug that drives the rest of the plot is given an origin story in three lines, and its colour is a wound. 'Love-in-idleness' is a real country name for the wild pansy, so the enchantment arrives dressed as folklore rather than as sorcery — which is how the play prefers its magic.

quotations.text: I'll put a girdle round about the earth In forty minutes.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Sent to fetch the flower from wherever it grows.
quotations.analysis: The boast fixes the scale of the wood: the errand crosses the world and takes less time than an act. It also quietly sets the play's clock against the audience's, since forty minutes is roughly how long the fairies are then offstage.

quotations.text: I am your spaniel; and, Demetrius, The more you beat me, I will fawn on you: Use me but as your spaniel, spurn me, strike me, Neglect me, lose me; only give me leave, Unworthy as I am, to follow you.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Pursuing Demetrius into the wood after he has told her to go away.
quotations.analysis: Four imperatives in a row, all of them asking to be hurt, and the one thing she requests is permission rather than affection. Oberon overhears this, which is why he intervenes — the play's only act of supernatural kindness is provoked by a woman debasing herself in front of a stranger.

quotations.text: Your wrongs do set a scandal on my sex: We cannot fight for love, as men may do; We should be wood and were not made to woo.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: After Demetrius threatens to do her mischief in the wood.
quotations.analysis: She identifies the rule she is breaking and states the cost of breaking it in one couplet. 'Wood' puns on wooed and on the old word for mad, and also names the place she is standing in — three meanings in a monosyllable, all of them about a woman who has come to the wrong place to do the wrong thing.

quotations.text: reason and love keep little company together now-a-days; the more the pity that some honest neighbours will not make them friends.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Replying to the fairy queen's declaration of love, while wearing an ass's head.
quotations.analysis: The play's thesis is delivered in prose by the only character who has not been given the drug, and he treats the failure of reason and love as a neighbourly dispute that a bit of mediation might settle. It is also a polite way of telling a queen that she is not making sense.

quotations.text: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Watching the four lovers converge, having caused the confusion himself.
quotations.analysis: The line is usually quoted as detached wisdom; on stage it is an author admiring his own mistake. Puck has just proposed that they stay and watch, which makes the lovers' worst hour into an entertainment with two spectators — the same arrangement the audience is in.

quotations.text: So we grow together, Like to a double cherry, seeming parted, But yet an union in partition; Two lovely berries moulded on one stem;
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Accusing Hermia of joining the men in mocking her.
quotations.analysis: The most tender description of friendship in the play is made in the course of ending one, and every image in it is of two things that cannot be separated. 'Union in partition' is a paradox held together only by the grammar, which is what the friendship has become by this point in the night.

quotations.text: O, when she's angry, she is keen and shrewd! She was a vixen when she went to school; And though she be but little, she is fierce.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Hiding behind the men as Hermia loses her temper.
quotations.analysis: The line most often printed on posters is an insult delivered while retreating, and the evidence for it is what Hermia was like at school — the two women have known each other since childhood and are now using that knowledge as ammunition. Hermia's reply picks out the only word that matters to her: 'Little' again.

quotations.text: My Oberon! what visions have I seen! Methought I was enamour'd of an ass.
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Waking after Oberon has taken the changeling boy and released her.
quotations.analysis: She calls it a vision, he says nothing about what he did, and the boy is never mentioned again by either of them. Her next line — that her eyes now loathe his visage — is aimed at a man asleep three feet away, and the comedy depends on the audience finding that funny rather than looking at it too closely.

quotations.text: The eye of man hath not heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man's hand is not able to taste, his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream was.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Alone on stage, waking after the others have gone.
quotations.analysis: The senses have been shuffled, which is exactly right for someone describing an experience the available vocabulary does not cover; the pattern is a garbled echo of St Paul on what the eye has not seen. The mangling is the meaning — this is the only character who admits that something happened which cannot be tidied into a morning story.

quotations.text: The lunatic, the lover and the poet Are of imagination all compact:
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Dismissing the lovers' account of the night before the entertainment begins.
quotations.analysis: 'All compact' means made entirely of, so the three are not compared but identified. The speech is the rational case against everything the audience has just watched, delivered by a character out of Greek myth in a play with fairies in it, and Hippolyta's reply — that all four tell the same story — is the only answer it gets.

quotations.text: And as imagination bodies forth The forms of things unknown, the poet's pen Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: He intends this as evidence that poets are unreliable, and produces the best description of writing in Shakespeare while doing it. 'A local habitation and a name' is what a stage gives a story — an address and a cast list — so the sceptic accidentally states the terms on which the theatre he is standing in operates.

quotations.text: The best in this kind are but shadows; and the worst are no worse, if imagination amend them.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Answering Hippolyta's complaint that the mechanicals' play is the silliest stuff she ever heard.
quotations.analysis: The defence of bad acting is also a defence of all acting, and it is made by the man who has just explained that imagination is not to be trusted. Hippolyta's answer is the sharper one: then it must be your imagination and not theirs, which puts the work of the theatre squarely on the people watching.

quotations.text: If we shadows have offended, Think but this, and all is mended, That you have but slumber'd here While these visions did appear.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: The epilogue, spoken after the fairies have blessed the house.
quotations.analysis: 'Shadows' is Theseus's word for actors four hundred lines earlier, so the epilogue picks up the court's own dismissal and turns it into an apology. The offer is the one the characters have already accepted about themselves — call it a dream — and the rhymed tetrameter is the fairies' metre, which means the excuse is being made by the people who caused the trouble.

timeline.label: The play probably written
timeline.detail: Usually placed in the mid-1590s on stylistic grounds, close to Romeo and Juliet; no document fixes the year.

timeline.label: Francis Meres lists the play in Palladis Tamia
timeline.detail: The earliest external record that it existed, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto, printed for Thomas Fisher
timeline.detail: The title page says the play had been publicly acted by the Lord Chamberlain's Men. Most modern editions descend from this text.

timeline.label: Second Quarto, falsely dated 1600
timeline.detail: Set from Q1 and belonging to the group of reprints associated with Thomas Pavier.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, from the second quarto, with small changes including the substitution of Egeus for Philostrate in the last act.

timeline.label: Samuel Pepys sees the play and detests it
timeline.detail: His diary records one of the bluntest hostile verdicts in the play's reception history.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn composes the overture
timeline.detail: Written when he was seventeen, and still the music most audiences hear in their heads.

timeline.label: Madame Vestris stages the play at Covent Garden
timeline.detail: A production that helped establish the Victorian fairy-spectacle tradition.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn's incidental music
timeline.detail: Added sixteen years after the overture, and the source of the wedding march.

timeline.label: Reinhardt and Dieterle's Hollywood film
timeline.detail: With James Cagney as Bottom and Mickey Rooney as Puck: the play as a studio fantasy.

timeline.label: Britten's opera premieres at Aldeburgh
timeline.detail: The libretto begins in the wood rather than in Athens, shifting the balance from law to enchantment.

timeline.label: Peter Brook's white box production for the RSC
timeline.detail: Sally Jacobs's bare white set, trapezes and circus skills replaced painted foliage and changed how the play could look.

places.name: Athens
places.note: Theseus's city, where the law gives a father the right to dispose of his daughter.

places.name: Sparta
places.note: Named by Theseus and Hippolyta when they compare hunting dogs on the morning after.

places.name: Crete
places.note: Where Hippolyta once heard hounds bay a bear, in the same exchange.

places.name: Thessaly
places.note: The third of the hunting regions Theseus lists when boasting about his pack.

places.name: India
places.note: The changeling boy's country, and the spiced Indian air where Titania's votaress laughed at the sails.

places.name: Fleet Street, London
places.note: Thomas Fisher's shop at the sign of the White Hart, where the 1600 quarto was sold.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest account reads the comedy as an entertainment for an aristocratic marriage, pointing to the three weddings, the blessing of the house and the compliment to a virgin queen in Oberon's speech about the imperial votaress.
criticalViews.counter: No record connects it to any particular wedding, and the 1600 title page advertises public performance; the theory explains the ending but not the cruelty of Act III.

criticalViews.summary: Criticism and production since the middle of the twentieth century have emphasised the coercion in the play: a father demanding a death sentence, a husband drugging his wife, a woman asking to be beaten, and an ending that leaves one man enchanted.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far enough it makes the last act unplayable, and has to treat the mechanicals' comedy as an interruption rather than as the answer the play gives.

criticalViews.summary: A third reading takes Pyramus and Thisbe as the centre: the comedy examines what an audience agrees to do, and the epilogue makes that agreement explicit.
criticalViews.counter: It can turn the lovers into a device and leave the fairy marriage — the one quarrel with consequences for crops and weather — as decoration.

essayQuestions.question: How does the wood change the people who enter it?
essayQuestions.focus: Transformation, law and the limits of magic
plan: Establish what Athens is: a city with a law that can kill a daughter, and a duke who enforces it in the first scene.
Show that the lovers' behaviour in the wood exaggerates what they already do — Helena betrays Hermia before any magic is used.
Read Bottom's transformation against Titania's: one is visible and harmless, the other invisible and humiliating.
Use 4.1 to ask what actually gets undone, and note that Demetrius is never released from the flower.
Conclude on the return to Athens: the law is not repealed, only set aside by a ruler in a good mood.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of women in the play.
essayQuestions.focus: Consent, friendship and the cost of the happy ending
plan: Begin with Hippolyta, won by the sword, and Hermia, offered a husband or a death, both in the first two hundred lines.
Trace Helena's self-abasement in 2.1 and ask what the play does with it: Oberon's pity, and no other consequence.
Use the double-cherry speech in 3.2 to show a friendship of years destroyed in a single scene, and by whom.
Examine Titania's account of the votaress: the one female relationship in the play that is not a rivalry, and the one that is broken offstage.
Weigh the three marriages of Act V against the means by which each was arranged.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of the mechanicals and their play?
plan: Describe the rehearsal problems of 1.2 and 3.1 as real problems for a real company: casting, fright, the boy playing a woman.
Note that Pyramus and Thisbe is the plot of Romeo and Juliet and very nearly the plot of the lovers' night.
Show how their over-explaining — a man playing Wall, a man apologising for the lion — exposes the conventions the surrounding play relies on.
Read the court's heckling in 5.1 and Theseus's 'the best in this kind are but shadows' as a statement about all acting.
Close with Hippolyta's correction: the imagination that mends a bad play belongs to the audience, not the actors.

essayQuestions.question: 'The comedy ends by asking everyone to call the night a dream.' How satisfying is that ending?
plan: Collect the waking scenes of 4.1 and note how little the lovers can retrieve and how readily they let it go.
Set Theseus's explanation of lunatic, lover and poet against Hippolyta's objection that four people agree.
Use Bottom's speech as the one refusal to tidy the experience into an account.
Consider what is left unresolved: the changeling boy, Egeus, Demetrius's enchantment.
Finish with Puck's epilogue, which offers the audience the same bargain the characters accepted, and decide whether taking it is a comfort or an evasion.

discussionQuestions: Demetrius is still under the spell at the end. Does that spoil the comedy, or is it the point of it?
Oberon drugs his wife into loving a man with an ass's head in order to win a custody dispute. Can the play be staged without that being cruel?
Helena asks to be treated like a dog. What is an audience supposed to feel during that speech?
The mechanicals perform the tragedy the lovers only just avoided. Why does Shakespeare put it at the end rather than the beginning?
Theseus says imagination cannot be trusted, in a play with fairies in it. Who wins that argument?

related.why: Written at about the same time, with the same plot of parental prohibition and mistaken death — played straight instead of as farce.
The other play of spirits, spells and interrupted entertainments, with the magic put to the business of government.
The other comedy in which leaving the city for a wood rearranges everybody's affections.
Desire misdirected without any magic at all, which makes a useful control on this play's flower.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller textual, critical and performance material.
